documentation.range:
Mainland Leopard Cat is one of the most widely distributed cat species in the world with its distribution ranging from the Russian Far East in the north to Singapore in the south.

Afghanistan: Afghanistan is the westernmost limit of the Mainland Leopard Cat’s global distribution range. The cat has been confirmed from Kunar, Nangarhar and Nuristan provinces (Habibi 2003, Stevens et al. 2011). One positive DNA sample also indicates its presence in Takhar province in north-east Afghanistan (Ostrowski et al. 2008).

Bangladesh: The Mainland Leopard Cat is present in all major forest ecosystems of Bangladesh: Eastern mixed-evergreen forests of Sylhet and Chattogram Hill Tracts; central, north and north-western dipterocarp-dominated deciduous forests and in the Sundarbans mangrove forests in south-western corner of the country. It is a matter of discussion whether the species has the widest distribution (second to Jungle Cat Felis chaus) in the country as stated by Ahmed (2015). Based on Ahmed et al. (2009), Khan (2008, 2018), and Khan (2010, 2015), it appears that the Mainland Leopard Cat in Bangladesh is very likely to be restricted to forested areas.

Bhutan: The Mainland Leopard Cat is a habitat generalist and can be found across the country, both in protected areas and outside. It has been reported from the sub-tropical jungles in the southern parts of the country to the alpine areas in the north above 4,000 m. The species has been recorded in Jigme Dorji National Park (Thinley et al. 2015, Jamtsho et al. 2021), Jigme Singye Wangchuck National Park (Wang and Macdonald 2009), Royal Manas National Park (Dhendup et al. 2016, Ghosh and Lucas 2017) and Lamai Goempa Research Preserve (Dhendup et al. 2019). Outside protected areas published records come from Gedu Division in the west, Sarpang Division in the south central, and Bumthang Division in Central Bhutan (Dhendup and Dorji 2018, Tenzin et al. 2019). The species has also been reported from Thimphu, Samtse, and Trashigang (Unpublished data with Tashi Dhendup)

Cambodia: The Mainland Leopard Cat appears to be widespread throughout Cambodia’s remaining forests. Recent camera-trap records (2010-onwards) confirm the species’ presence in most of Cambodia’s major biodiversity conservation landscapes, including the Cardamom Mountains Landscape (e.g., Botum Sakor National Park, Central Cardamom Mountains National Park, Phnom Samkos Wildlife Sanctuary, Southern Cardamom National Park, Gray et al. 2017; Peam Krasop Wildlife Sanctuary, Ream National Park, Prey Nub, Thuang et al. 2017), the Eastern Plains Landscape (i.e., Keo Seima Wildlife Sanctuary, Griffin et al. 2020; Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary, Pin et al. 2018), the Northern Plains Landscape (e.g., Chheb Wildlife Sanctuary, Kulen Promtep Wildlife Sanctuary, Phnom Tbeng Natural Heritage Site, Preah Rokar Wildlife Sanctuary, Techo Sen Russey Treb Cambodian Royal Academy National Park, Griffin et al. 2020), the Prey Lang Forest Landscape (e.g., Prey Lang Wildlife Sanctuary, Hayes et al. 2015), the Tonle Sap Floodplains (e.g., Tonle Sap Biosphere Reserve, Griffin et al. 2020), and the Tri-Border Forest (e.g. Siem Pang Wildlife Sanctuary, Loveridge et al. 2018; Virachey National Park, McCann et al. 2020).

China: The Mainland Leopard Cat is present in Guangxi autonomous region, Hainan island, Guizhou, Sichuan, Tibet, Yunnan, Hebei, Heilongjang, Henan, Jiangsu, Jilin, Liaoning, Nei Mongol, Shandong, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Qinghai, Hunan, Hubei, Beijing and Zhejiang provinces (Wang et al. 2019, Jinping 2010, Sheng et al. 2010, Yu 2010, Bu et al. 2016, Shi et al. 2017, Jia et al. 2020, Li et al. 2019, 2020, Liu et al. 2020). Fujian province and Jiangxi province also have documented Mainland Leopard Cat presence within China (Jiang et al. 2021).

India: The Mainland Leopard Cat is among the most common small wild cats in India, with a large distribution. It occurs across the Western Ghats, along the higher elevation areas of the eastern hills and the coastal belt, north-east India, in the Terai and the Duars, and the Himalaya. Due to lack of systematic surveys in the eastern hill regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh and the adjoining regions of Chhattisgarh, its distribution in these areas remains poorly documented. Of the 28 states in India, it has confirmed presence in at least 21 states, and one Union Territory.

Some of the sites in India where the species has been reported from include:

Himalaya: Dachigam NP, Kashmir (Mukherjee et al. 2010, Noor et al. 2020); Khangchendzonga Biosphere Reserve, Sikkim (Bashir et al. 2014); several locations in Himachal Pradesh (Mukherjee et al. 2010) including Kinnaur at around 3000±400 m elevation (Suryawanshi, K.S., pers. comm.).

Terai, Duars, and the foothills of the Himalaya: Rajaji TR, Corbett TR, Katerniaghat WLS, Dudhwa TR, Valmiki TR, Buxa TR (Jhala et al. 2020).

North-east India:

a) Arunachal Pradesh: Eaglenest WLS (Velho et al. 2015, Mukherjee et al. 2016), Namdapha TR (Datta et al. 2008, Jhala et al. 2020), Kamlang WLS (Jhala et al. 2020), Dibang WLS (S. Nijhawan pers. comm.), Pakke TR (Selvan et al. 2014, Mukherjee et al. 2019, Jhala et al. 2020), Talle Valley WLS (Mukherjee et al. 2019), Singchung-Bugun CCR (Mukherjee et al. 2019)

b) Nagaland: Intanki NP (Longchar 2013), Shatuya Forest (Grewal et al. 2013), Dzükou Valley (Joshi et al. 2019)

c) Mizoram: Dampa TR (Singh and Macdonald 2017, Mukherjee et al. 2019, Jhala et al. 2020) and Thorangtlang WLS (P. Singh pers. comm.)

d) Assam: Manas NP (Goswami and Ganesh 2011); Kaziranga NP, Orang NP, Nameri TR (Jhala et al. 2020), Jaypore FD (Wildlife Conservation Society 2010), Dibru-Saikhowa NP (Mukherjee et al. 2019); Bornadi-Khalingduar Complex (Chakraborty et al. 2015)

e) Meghalaya: Nongkhyllem WLS and Baghmara-Balpakram landscape (Mukherjee et al. 2019),

Eastern coastal areas: Sundarbans TR (Das et al. 2012, Jhala et al. 2020), Bhitarkanika WLS (Palei et al. 2018)

Eastern Ghats: Simlipal TR (Palei et al. 2015), Satkosia TR, Papikonda NP (Aditya and Ganesh 2016). In this region, the area between Papikonda and Satkosia-Simlipal remains poorly surveyed. An unverified record from Koratput exists however, this area requires more field surveys to accurately determine the distribution of this species.

Western Ghats: Anshi-Dandeli TR, Bandipur TR, Bhadra TR, Nagarahole TR, Biligiri Rangaswamy Temple TR (Mukherjee et al. 2010, Kumara et al. 2012, Kumara et al. 2014, Srivathsa et al. 2015), Kalakad-Mundanthurai TR (Mudappa et al. 2007), Mudumalai TR, Sathyamangalam TR, Parambikulam TR (Sreehari and Nameer 2016), Periyar TR (Mukherjee et al. 2010, Jhala et al. 2020), Eravikulam NP (Nikhil and Nameer 2017), Peppara WLS (Jayson and Christopher 1995), Silent Valley NP (Mukherjee et al. 2010, Sanghamitra and Nameer 2018), Anamalai TR (Kumaraguru et al. 2011), Wayanad WLS (Sreekumar and Nameer 2018). An unverified record of a road kill from near Bhandardara in Maharashtra also exists, extending the possible distribution of leopard cats in the Western Ghats further north.

Mammal checklists from Keoladeo Ghana WLS (Singh et al. 2017) and the Damodar River Valley in Jharkhand (Chakraborty 2011) also include the Mainland Leopard Cat. However, in the absence of photographic evidence of this cat from these areas, the veracity of these records remains unsubstantiated.

Japan: The Mainland Leopard Cat is the only wild felid in Japan (Ross et al. 2015). Small populations inhabit the Island of Tsushima (only found in the Tsushima area of Nagasaki Prefecture) and of Iriomote (Ross et al. 2015, Schmidt et al. 1987).

Lao PDR: There is very little survey involving Mainland Leopard Cats in Lao PDR and much of what occurs is associated with development projects and results are not made publicly available. The species’ current distribution in the country is largely unknown. Given Lao PDR’s relatively high forest cover (~57% of total land cover, Department of Forestry 2018) and the leopard cat’s tolerance of human disturbance, it is likely that the species is widespread throughout the country. However, given the occurrence of indiscriminate wire-snaring throughout Lao PDR it is conceivable that the species has been extirpated from some parts of the country, particularly those where habitat is heavily fragmented and trade-driven snaring is intense. Recent published camera-trap records (2010-onwards) confirm the species’s presence in Nakai-Nam Theun National Park (Association Anoulak 2019), Nam Et Phou Louey National Biodiversity Conservation Area (Rasphone et al. 2019), Nam Kading National Biodiversity Area (Wildlife Conservation Society, unpubl. data), Phou Hin Poun National Protected Area (Brakels and Somdachit 2020), and in Xe Sap National Protected Area and adjacent Palé Watershed Protection Forest (Tilker et al. 2019). Many other unpublished locality records exist spread across the country, with no obvious gaps in terms of camera-trapping of appropriate intensity failing to find the species in any survey area however these records are not systematically collated by the concerned people owing to its least conservation concern status by IUCN (J. W. Duckworth pers. comm. 2021)

Malaysia: The species has been recorded throughout Malaysia, including Mersing and Panti Forest Reserves in Johor, Sungai Yu Forest Reserve and Taman Negara National Park in Pahang, Pasoh Forest Reserve in Negeri Sembilan, Gunung Inas Forest Reserve in Kedah and in Dungun Timber Complex, Tembat Forest Reserve and Petuang Forest Reserve Terrenganu (Gumal et al. 2014, Ross et al. 2015, Magintan et al. 2017, Ota et al. 2020, Clements et al. 2021). Since the presence of both Mainland Leopard Cat and Sunda Leopard Cat is expected in the peninsular Malaysia it is difficult to be certain on exact distribution of Mainland Leopard Cats within the peninsula (Patel et al. 2017).

Myanmar: The Mainland Leopard Cat is the most widespread small cat in Myanmar occurring in almost all regions of the country including the states of Kachin, Kayin, Sagaing, Shan, Rakhine, Mandalay and Bago (Moo et al. 2017). Locality wise it has been recorded from Alaungadaw Kathapa National Park, Tanintharyi Nature Reserve and Shwesettaw Wildlife Sanctuary (Linnell et al. 2014). Than Zaw et al. (2014) confirmed the presence of leopard cat from southernmost to the northernmost areas, within 151 independent camera-trap detection events coming from 15 survey areas.It is also well distributed in Htamanthi Wildlife Sanctuary (HlaNaing et al. 2019), Hukaung Valley (HlaNaing 2015) and Myitsone, Lai Zar, proposed Tanintharyi National Park, Tachileik, Minlar, Alaungdaw Kathapa National Park (SuSu 2005), Karen State (Moo et al. 2018) and Eastern Shan State (MONREC 2020).

Nepal: The Mainland Leopard Cat has been confirmed from 31 out of 77 districts. These include Arghakhanchi, Baglung, Bajura, Banke, Bardia, Bhaktapur, Bhojpur, Chitwan, Dadeldhura (Acharya, B. pers. comm. 2020), Dang (C. Khanal pers. comm. 2020), Gorkha, Gulmi, Jajarkot, Jhapa, Jumla, Kavrepalanchowk, Kailali, Kalikot, Kanchanpur, Kapilvastu, Kaski, Kathmandu, Khotang, Lamjung, Mahottari, Mugu, Myagdi, Okhaldhunga, Palpa, Parbat, Parsa, Rasuwa, Rupandehi, Sankhuwasabha, Saptari, Solukhumbu, Surkhet, Syangja, Taplejung, Terhathum and Udayapur (FON Nepal 2020, Himalayan Nature 2018, FON Nepal 2017, Ghimirey 2017, Thapa et al. 2013, Jnawali et al. 2011). Confirmed records for the species have been made from the protected areas of Annapurna Conservation Area, Banke National Park, Bardia National Park, Chitwan National Park, Gaurishankar Conservation Area, Kanchenjunga Conservation Area, Manaslu Conservation Area, Makalu Barun National Park, Parsa National Park, Rara National Park, Shivapuri-Nagarjuna National Park and Shuklaphanta National Park (Poudyal et al. 2019, Appel et al. 2013, Thapa et al. 2013, Ghimirey et al. 2012, Jnawali et al. 2011, Pandey 2010). The species has been even recorded to have been using the alpine habitat in eastern Nepal at 4,474 m (Thapa et al. 2013).

Pakistan: In Pakistan, this cat species is found in the Murree hills and the Kaghan valley (Khatoon et al. 2019). It also occurs in Azad Jammu and Kashmir. Further west it is found in Swat, Dir, and lower Gilgit through Hazara District and lower Chitral (Roberts 1997). There are conflicting reports about its occurrence in other areas of northern Pakistan.

Russia: The Mainland Leopard Cat inhabits the Far East region of the Russia (Primorskii Krai), both in protected areas and outside. The species is regularly registered in the forest area and flat river open valleys, and also near villages in landscapes influenced by agricultural work in the south-eastern region of the country (in the border of Russia and China, of Russia and DPR Korea). Protected areas inhabited by the Mainland Leopard Cat include Leopard Land and Ussuriiskii Nature Reserve, Sikhote-Alin Nature Reserve, Lazovsky Nature Reserve, Khankaiskii Nature Reserve and Bolshekhekhtsirskii Nature Reserve (Yudin 2015).

Singapore: In Singapore, the Leopard Cat is found in the remnant major forest fragments on the main island of Singapore and two offshore islands of Tekong and Ubin (Chua et al. 2016). Leopard Cats in Singapore are phenotypically closer to the Mainland Leopard Cat however the similarity of their cytochrome b with Sunda leopard cat makes it uncertain on the species of leopard cat in the country and their distribution (Chua 2013).

Republic of Korea: The Mainland Leopard Cat is widespread across the Republic of Korea, except on the small offshore islands (Kim et al. 2021). From the island Jeju, it disappeared between 1930 and 1940 (Kim et al. 2021).

Taiwan: The Mainland Leopard Cat was once widespread in lowland regions of Taiwan but its population has been greatly reduced (Chen et al. 2016). Its distribution is now restricted to areas in the counties of Miaoli, Nantou and Taichung City in Central Taiwan (Chen et al. 2019).

Thailand: The Mainland Leopard cat is widespread in Thailand’s forests; with many recent records from both protected and non-protected areas throughout the country. Recent records (2010-onwards) confirm the species’s presence in most of Thailand’s major forest complexes (FC) such as Lum Nam Pai-Salawin FC (e.g., Salawin WS, Salawin WS unpubl. data), Western FC (e.g. Thung Yai Naresuan WS, Chutipong et al. 2016; Huai Kha Kaeng WS, N. Sukumal, unpubl. data; Mae Wong NP, WWF-Thailand unpubl. data; Khlong Lan NP; WWF-Thailand, unpubl. data; Khao Laem NP, Freeland Foundation 2019a), Kaeng Krachan FC (e.g., Namtok Huai Yang NP, Freeland Foundation 2019b; Kui Buri NP, N. Seuaturien, unpubl. data), Khlong Saeng-Khao Sok FC (e.g. Khlong Saeng WS and Khao Sok NP, Petersen et al. 2020), Hala Bala FC (e.g., Hala Bala WS, T. Dawrueng unpubl. data), Eastern FC (e.g., Khao Aung Rue Nai WS., Baker et al. 2015), Dong-Phayayen-Khao Yai FC (e.g., Dong Yai WS, Khao Yai NP, Pang Sida NP, Thap Lan NP, and Ta Phraya NP, Ash et al. 2020), Doi Phu Kha-Mae Yom FC (e.g. Tub Phaya Lor NHA, Wiang Lo WS, Doi Phu Nang NP, G. Saridnir ununpubl. data), and Phu Khieo-Nam Nao FC (e.g. Phu Khieo WS, A. Riggio unpubl. data), as well as several smaller forest fragments (e.g., Sakaerat Biosphere Reserve, Petersen et al. 2019a; Khao Sam RoiYot NP, K. Phosri unpubl. data; Pak Pha-Nang (Nakhon Si Thammarat Province), Thalae Noi (Phutthalung), ThaPhae (Satun), La-Un (Rangong), Koh Lanta (Krabi), Kantang and Bangsak (Trang), Khura Buri and Takua Pha (Phang Nga), Tantipisanuh et al. 2019; and Wang Mai (Chumphon), Ueda 2020).

Viet Nam: The Mainland Leopard Cat is currently the most widespread cat species in the country. Willcox et al. (2014) reported 32 occurrences of this species from various parts of the country. Not much targeted research on the species has yet been conducted in the country.

Hong Kong: The Mainland Leopard Cat is distributed mostly in the new territories in the north while it is presumably absent in the Lantau island in the south. Hong Kong island in the south is also inhabited by the species.
documentation.population:
Information on the Mainland Leopard Cat’s population status is limited despite the widespread use of camera-traps across the species’ geographic range. Its population has not been estimated in most parts of its range and there is little information on the abundance of this species except for some very small and isolated areas or specific protected areas where its estimates are often the result of bycatch data. This reflects the species’ low interest to researchers.

Despite the general paucity of information on the Mainland Leopard Cat population size and trends, the species is generally considered to be abundant and stable based on the following observations: (1) the Mainland Leopard Cat appears to be widely distributed throughout its historical geographic range and (2) it appears to tolerate human modified environments to a better degree than other sympatric cat species. However, this does not mean the species is invulnerable to habitat loss and degradation, as previous studies suggest the species is at least somewhat dependent on nearby forest cover and avoids large artificial open areas (e.g. non-woody agriculture) if vegetation cover is insufficient (e.g. Chen et al. 2016). Furthermore, any potentially detrimental effects of habitat loss and degradation will be exacerbated by illegal hunting, likely causing population declines in some regions. This is evident in parts of Southeast Asia where some Mainland Leopard Cat populations appear to have been negatively influenced due to ongoing wire-snaring crises (e.g. Coudrat et al. 2014a,b; Willcox et al. 2014).

Published spatial capture-recapture derived density estimates for this species vary substantially (2.9-21.42 individuals / 100 km2) and are currently available from only a few locations, making generalizations about broader population abundance difficult at this time. These include six locations in India: Pakke Tiger Reserve: 2.9/100 km2 (Selvan et al.2014), Biligiri Rangaswamy Temple Tiger Reserve: 4.48/100 km2 (Srivathsa et al.2015), Bhadra Tiger Reserve: 10.45 / 100 km2 (Srivathsa et al.2015) and Khangchendzonga Biosphere Reserve: 17.52/100 km2 (Bashir et al.2013), one from Nepal: Banke National Park: 4.85/100 km2 (Dhakal 2018) and one location in Thailand: Sakaerat Biosphere Reserve: 17.7/100 km2 (Petersen et al.2019b). The highest density for the species (89.4±17.2 (SE) individuals/100 km2) has been recorded from Tekong Island, Singapore (an estimate of 21 adults; Chua et al. 2016).

Mainland Leopard Cat population densities presumably vary by habitat type and level of human disturbance as those factors influence resource availability, foraging success, and the potential for inter-specific competition. Petersen et al.(2019b) found that Leopard Cat density varied by habitat type within a degraded forest fragment in north-eastern Thailand (Sakaerat Biosphere Reserve), being highest in semi-evergreen forest (21.42/100 km2), followed by mixed-acacia/eucalyptus plantation forest (7.9/100 km2). Detections were too few to estimate Leopard Cat density in the site’s third major forest type, dry dipterocarp forest. Spatial capture-recapture derived estimates of rodent biomass were highest in the semi-evergreen forest during the study period, followed by dry dipterocarp, and plantation forests (Petersen et al. 2019b). The potential for inter-specific competition between Leopard Cats and other sympatric small terrestrial carnivores was found to be greatest in the dry dipterocarp forest (Petersen et al. 2019a). Similarly, Srivathsa et al. (2015), using bycatch data from four camera-trap surveys targeting the Tiger (Panthera tigris) in the Western Ghats (India), found high Mainland Leopard Cat densities to be clustered around secondary, disturbed, or partly modified forests and human-use areas, and attributed the high leopard cat densities to presumably high rodent abundances in those same areas. Leopard Cat density estimates from core areas of larger, closer to intact forest landscapes, however, are lacking. Past studies from such areas have reported lower Mainland Leopard Cat photo-encounter rates than for some other sympatric felids (e.g. Petersen et al. 2020; with similar findings reported for the Sunda Leopard Cat (Prionailurus javanensis): McCarthy et al. 2015), suggesting the high Mainland Leopard Cat densities reported from smaller forest fragments and other disturbed locations should not be extrapolated to these less disturbed areas.

Country-specific reliable population estimates for the species are not available though several educated guesses have been made across its range. Not more than 1,600 individuals are believed to inhabit the whole range on the territory of Russia (Yudin 2015) while only fewer than 2,500 and 100-150 individuals are believed to exist in Nepal and Pakistan respectively (Jnawali et al. 2011). A total of around 50 individuals were estimated from Singapore. For the islands Iriomote and Tsushima in Japan and for Taiwan, the population sizes of the Mainland Leopard Cat are supposed to be very small (Ross et al. 2015). Khan (2015) and Khan (2018) both labelled the species as uncommon in Bangladesh. Population size or trends are not known for any other country. In China, the population size of the MLC is about 230,000, and the population trend is stable (Jiang et al. 2021).
documentation.habitats:
Mainland Leopard Cat inhabits a variety of habitats, from tropical rainforest to temperate broadleaf forest and marginally, coniferous forest, as well as shrub forest and successional grasslands (Thapa et al. 2013, Ghimirey et al. 2012, Shrivathsa et al. 2015, Coudrat et al. 2014). It also occurs in mountainous areas, lowland riparian habitats and agricultural wetlands (Kim et al. 2021). They are also known to adapt to a variety of habitats including monoculture like coffee, tea, rubber and palm plantations (Bali et al. 2007, Kumara et al. 2004, Tweedie 1978, Yu 2010, Nick Baker in litt. November 2021). Their adaptability to agricultural landscapes and plantations is often attributed to presence of rodents as prey in such habitats (Lim 1999). They are frequently reported along roads and human settlements. They have been recorded in the Himalayas as high as 4,474 m (Thapa et al.2013). Home range of leopard cat varies from 1.5 to 12.4 km2 (Chen et al. 2016).

Mainland Leopard Cats prey primarily upon rodents like squirrels, rats and mice, ground birds and lizards. A total of 63 species of prey were found in their scats in Primorsky region of Russia with mammals and birds having highest frequency (89.3% and 30.6%) in their diet (Seryodkin and Burkovskiy 2019). They have been found to be mostly nocturnal and crepuscular (Can et al. 2019, Chua et al. 2016, Mukherjee et al. 2019, Petersen et al. 2019a).

In the wild, birth dens have been found in hollow trees, amongst bushes, under overhanging rocks in small caves, under big roots, and between rocks. They are also excellent swimmers, and show an affinity towards water (Yu 2010). Available evidence from Thailand suggests Mainland Leopard Cat habitat use and activity patterns might be influenced by a combination of resource availability and inter-specific competition. Petersen et al. (2019a) found Leopard Cat habitat use within a forest fragment in north-eastern Thailand was positively associated with rodent biomass during a period of resource scarcity. However, no association was found between Leopard Cat habitat use and rodent biomass during a subsequent period of high rodent biomass.
documentation.threats:
Potential threats to Mainland Leopard Cat vary across its geographic range, but overall, there is no evidence of any serious threats operating over large areas. Hunting and snaring occur in most parts of Mainland Leopard Cat’s range and is particularly intense in South-east Asia (Gray et al. 2018, Harrison et al. 2016, Willcox et al. 2014). But surveys in areas affected by heavy snaring show the Mainland Leopard Cat to be one of the most resilient species of small carnivores (Willcox et al. 2014). Hence there is little evidence to suggest that hunting and/or snaring is reducing Mainland Leopard Cat’s population at a global scale. The species is traded or hunted for meat in parts of north-east India (Selvan et al. 2013), in parts of Afghanistan (Karlstetter 2008), Bangladesh (S. Chaudhary pers. comm. 2021) and in South-east Asia (Willcox et al. 2014) but there is no evidence that this practice has dramatically reduced the species’ populations in those areas. A recent report shows that from North China to Sichuan, from Jiangxi to Yunnan, and areas like Guangxi and Guangdong showed a lower than expected number of wild Mainland Leopard Cat. The contributing reason behind the population decline in southern China is believed to be hunting for food and fur, however, more recently evidence shows illegal adoption, domestication, and hybrid breeding of Bengal Leopard Cat maybe other main factors (CFCA 2017). In recent years, the data indicate that the hunting pressure on the Chinese Mainland Leopard Cat populations has been dramatically reduced (Yu 2010). Additionally, China’s massive natural forest protection campaign since 1998 may also be very helpful for habitat recovery, which should be beneficial for the Leopard Cat (Yu 2010).

Retaliatory killings in response to perceived poultry depredation are common though not at a rate to threaten its population either locally or globally. Misidentifications (as, for example mistaking the species as Leopard Panthera pardus or Snow Leopard Panthera uncia cub or Fishing Cat Prionailurus viverrinus) leading to lethal anthropogenic responses are common in countries like Bangladesh and Nepal. These perspectives instil fear, resulting in stern retaliatory anthropogenic responses however most of these responses are few and far between, with little impact in the global or even local scale.

Deforestation is potentially an important driver of habitat deterioration and may be a localised threat to Mainland Leopard Cat survival in certain areas such as the eastern Afghanistan. Habitat loss or deterioration from other countries in its range has also been documented. Also, a recent study using ecological niche models suggests that the primary macroscale factors that negatively impact Leopard Cat are, climate change and human induced habitat degradation (Silva et al. 2020). However, its occurrence in areas without actual forests indicates that this is less of a threat than previously perceived. In Thailand, it is presumed to have higher mortality due to increased proximity to humans (Haines et al. 2004), but recent research in China shows much better adaptation by the species to human disturbance (Wu et al. 2018). The species’ overall tolerance to human disturbance allows for a much wider population of the species than would be the case if it inhabited in areas infrequented by humans. The species’ ability to disperse between the many isolated forest fragments in which it currently occurs is unknown, though available evidence suggests it may be limited in Taiwan (Chen et al. 2016). By contrast, in southern Korea, the species disperses freely across non-forest landscapes as shown by its strong colonisation of newly-reclaimed areas of formerly intertidal habitat converted to rice fields and brackish wetlands. In principle, inter-patch dispersal ability depends on the structure and composition of the surrounding matrix and overall landscape permeability, features that can be both site- and period-specific (Metzger and Décamps 1997). As such, the long-term viability of isolated populations living within many forest fragments is uncertain and probably variable.

Free roaming dogs, Feline Immunodeficiency Virus (FIV) transmission from feral cats and reduced prey availability can also threaten the Mainland Leopard Cat in specific areas, such as for example the population on Tsushima island, Japan (Ministry of the Environment of the Government of Japan, no date). Protoparvovirus have also been found in Mainland Leopard Cat in China (Chen et al. 2019). Road kills in and around protected areas and forests is another visible potential issue for the Mainland Leopard Cat in some areas (Kim et al. 2019, Chen et al. 2016, Baskaran and Bhoominathan 2010, Izawa et al. 2009), though it is presumably not a prominent overall threat at the moment.
documentation.measures:
Conservation measures tailored to the Mainland Leopard Cat are scarce, except the protected areas which provide safe refuge to the species, often under the umbrella of other keystone species. Generally, its population trend and status is not well known. In Afghanistan and Pakistan, the Leopard Cat is data deficient, hence the first concrete steps in these countries would be the systematic assessment of the species’ current range, abundance and threats. Its status in other countries of its geographic range is relatively more common though a comprehensive assessment in China regarding the illegal trade of the species would be a good step. In China, the species has been listed as Category II of National Key Protected Wild Animals (2021). The populations of the species in nature reserves are under protection, and it has been listed as Vulnerable in the China's Red List of Biodiversity (Jiang et al. 2021). Systematic monitoring of potential threats to the species is really the primary need, in case any of them should change into serious threats.

Generally, the species is widely reported and presumably abundant in Nepal, India, Malaysia, Myanmar and Thailand. Thus, dedicated conservation measures targeting this species are rare in these countries. One of the important conservation initiatives for the Mainland Leopard Cat includes enlisting the species in the schedule I of National Park and Wildlife Conservation Act 1973 in Nepal. The species is also protected in Bangladesh, included in schedule I of the Wildlife (Conservation and Protection) Act 2012. Myanmar too has provided complete protection to the species according to the newly updated Conservation of Biodiversity and Protected Area Law (2018). In Japan the species has been declared a National Nature Monument in 1971 and an endangered species in 1994 and a conservation project plan has been initiated since 1995. The species is listed in the schedule I of the Forest and Nature Conservation Act of Bhutan 1995. Hence, hunting or trade of any sort is completely prohibited in the country.

Since the species is not highly sought after by researchers it will be a great initiative if researchers from across its global range collaborate to produce a range-wide estimation of its habitat suitability including the already existing presence data of the species.
documentation.use_trade: Mainland Leopard Cat’s involvement in illegal wildlife trade is not properly known from most parts of its range. However there have been many documented cases of this species in trade or hunted for meat in parts of north-east India, South-east Asia and China. The species is, for example, hunted as meat by indigenous tribes in Chattogram Hill Tracts (S. C. Rahman and S. Chakma pers. comm. 2020). According to Karlstetter (2008, pers. comm. with C. Miller), the Leopard Cat is the second most abundant of all cat species listed for Afghanistan at Kabul’s fur Market, and the same author reported pelts of Leopard Cat in Nuristan Province, although it was not specified whether they had been hunted specifically for fur trade or as retaliatory killing. A Kabul household consumption survey also confirmed that Leopard Cats continue to be hunted and their pelts traded (Jonson and Wingard 2010). Cross-border trade across Afghanistan and Pakistan has also been documented (Bader et al. 2013, Ostrowski et al. 2009). Even though hundreds of thousands were trapped for the fur trade in the 1980s, Leopard Cat still seems to be fairly common in the first decade of the 21st century. However, in China there was a decline in harvest of legal trapping which was an indication for over-hunting (Yu 2010). For many decades, some border town markets in Myanmar like Tachileik have sold various body parts, which are mostly pelts (Nijman et al. 2015). In addition, Leopard Cats were the second most common species found in wildlife trade markets of Tachileik and Mong La in Myanmar-Thailand border based on the total number of individual skins encountered (458 skins) while they were the most abundant considering number of individuals per survey (median 26 individuals/survey; Nijmann and Shepherd 2015). Body parts have also been seized in Nepal though the frequency of seizure is too little to indicate any serious threats to the Mainland Leopard Cat population in the country (Dangol 2015). Their fur and meat are especially popular in China and Japan, which played a major role in the decrease of the population in China in earlier decades. They are also popular in the pet trade industry, as they are often bred with domestic cats to create Bengal cats (Chan 2010). Illegal trade in this species using the internet is also known from Vietnam (Nguyen and Willemsen 2016).
documentation.rationale:
The Mainland Leopard Cat is widely reported and appears to be common across its large geographic range. Despite this, little is actually known concerning the species' global population size and status (i.e., declining, stable, increasing). Absolute abundance estimates available from only a handful of sites might not properly represent its population across its global range, however indicate good population in those surveyed sites. Thus, we believe the species warrants the treatment of Least Concern, given how widely reported the species is and how good the population size is in the surveyed sites.

The habitat seems to be lost and/or modified in many regions (e.g. Hansen et al. 2013). However, an ability to adapt to different habitat types has helped its population to persist in those areas. There have been countries/regions too, for example Nepal which have experienced an increase in their forest cover (DFRS 2015). The Extent of Occurrence and the Area of Occupancy of the Mainland Leopard Cat are suspected to have remained more or less the same, and both are very much bigger than would be apt for categorisation as anything other than Least Concern.

Although there have certainly been localized declines, there are no indications of an overall global population decline by the species at a rate sufficient for categorisation as anything other than Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
In 2017, a taxonomic revision of all cat species recognized the split of the Leopard Cat into two different species: Mainland Leopard Cat (Prionailurus bengalensis) and Sunda Leopard Cat (Prionailurus javanensis). The Mainland Leopard Cat, meanwhile, has two recognized subspecies:
  • Prionailurus bengalensis bengalensis in South and Southeast Asia occurring from Pakistan to China and probably inhabiting the Malay Peninsula and
  • Prionailurus bengalensis euptilurus existing in Manchuria, Russian Far East, Taiwan, Iriomote Island and Tsushima Island.
The Iriomote Cat was widely and until recently treated as a species but is now, according to Kitchener et al. (2017), included into the subspecies Prionailurus bengalensis euptilurus.
